characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: EBSD system attached to field emission gun SEM (FEI Quanta 650, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Hillsboro, OR, USA); operating voltage 20 kV, step size 0.5 μm; specimens mechanically ground then electro-polished in 7% Nital at room temperature; Channel 5 post-processing software; grain size by linear intercept method with 15° boundary misorientation definition
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 0.6%C steel both FCC austenite and BCC ferrite (~30 vol%) are present; ferrite grain size ~5.5 μm, austenite grain size ~7.3 μm; twin boundary fraction f_Tw = 56.7%
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine phase distribution (FCC austenite / BCC ferrite), grain size and twin boundary arrangement as a function of alloying content

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: TEM (Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Hillsboro, OR, USA) operated at 200 kV; thin foils prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 20 V and −20 °C
characterization_methods.key_findings: Nano-sized κ-carbides smaller than 1 nm precipitated in the austenite of the 0.6%C steel, giving very weak κ diffraction spots; orientation relationship (001)κ || (001)γ; κ-carbide diameter 1.0 ± 0.4 nm
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: 200 kV; dark-field images taken along [001]γ zone axis using a κ-carbide reflection
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize κ-carbide size, distribution and orientation relationship in the austenite matrix
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) dark-field imaging and selected area electron diffraction (SAED)

analytical_models.equation_role: Predicts mass density (g/cm³) from C, Al and Mn content in mass%
analytical_models.model_note: ρ = 8.10 − 0.102C − 0.10Al − 0.01Mn; data for C plotted as 10× the experimental values in Fig. 6(b).

computational_details.simulation_method: Analytical linear least-squares fitting of density versus alloying content
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Density predicted from Eq. (3) for Fe30Mn11Al1.0C (6.6 g/cm³) and Fe30Mn11Al1.5C (6.55 g/cm³) matches experimental values (6.60 and 6.56 g/cm³), unlike previously reported coefficients.

analytical_models.equation_role: Gives the shear strength contribution σ_shear = α f^1/2 d_Car^1/2 from coherent κ-carbides
analytical_models.model_note: Shear strengthening remains active for κ-carbide sizes as large as 50 nm, well above the ~5 nm critical size for the shear-to-Orowan transition.

parameters.name: α
parameters.value: constant determined by the nature of the particle (not numerically given)

parameters.name: f
parameters.value: volume fraction of κ-carbides (not numerically given)

analytical_models.equation_role: Linear fits of R_p0.2 and R_m against the square root of κ-carbide diameter
analytical_models.model_name: Yield/tensile strength vs d_Car^0.5 linear fits (Fig. 7(a))
analytical_models.model_note: Yield strength shows the strongest dependence on κ-carbide size; strength after solution processing controlled mainly by κ-carbide size rather than grain size, ferrite fraction or twin-boundary fraction.

computational_details.simulation_method: Analytical model / linear fitting of mechanical properties versus square root of κ-carbide size
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Yield strength is linearly proportional to the square root of the κ-carbide size, giving a slope of 97.1 MPa/nm^1/2 and an intercept (no κ-carbide strengthening contribution) of about 478 MPa.

interfaces.interface_notes: The κ-carbides show very weak diffraction spots in SAED due to their fine size and short-range ordering of C and Al in the austenite; the coherent nature means their strengthening follows a shear mechanism.
interfaces.phase_evolution: Nano-sized κ-carbides (<1 nm at 0.6%C) precipitate in the austenite during solution treatment and coarsen with increasing carbon content.

phase_interfaces.coherence: coherent interface, evidenced by SAED observations; orientation relationship (001)κ || (001)γ

interfaces.slip_behavior: Shear deformation of the coherent κ-carbides facilitates the glide of dislocations across κ-carbide shear planes, resulting in a weakened work hardening; strengthening is by a particle shear model rather than an Orowan mechanism.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Each steel composition first melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace with a 50 kg capacity.
Cast into an ingot with a diameter of 150 mm.
Hot rolled into rods with a diameter of 16 mm.
Hot-rolled rods air-cooled to room temperature.
Hot-rolled rods solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching; the main final state (state_label 1050 °C–2 h–WQ) used for tensile, Charpy and EBSD/TEM characterization.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: MTS tensile machine; two solution-treated specimens tested and data is the average value of two specimens; after 1050 °C/2 h solution treatment
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: standard tensile specimen, gauge length 25 mm, diameter 5 mm, tensile axis parallel to the rod axis

fracture_strength_sigma_FS.note: σ_FS = fracture strength (highest local strength during tensile deformation)

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Room-temperature engineering stress-strain curve for the 0.6C steel (Fig. 2(a)); shows the strongest ductility and the highest work-hardening rate among the Fe30Mn11Al(x)C series, failing beyond ~55-63% strain

ultimate_true_stress_sigma_TS.note: σ_TS = maximum true stress just before necking (crack nucleation)

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: MTS impact tester (500 J capacity); two solution-treated specimens tested, data is the average value of two specimens
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: Charpy impact specimen cut from solution-treated rods with V-notch perpendicular to the rod axis

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: density measured by the Archimedes drainage method

phases_present.morphology: equiaxed austenite grains with abundant twin boundaries
phases_present.texture: twin boundary fraction f_Tw = 56.7% (fractional twin boundary length)

phases_present.morphology: thick elongated bands crossing the austenite grain structure (from Fig. 3(a))

precipitates.coherency: coherent interface with the austenite matrix; orientation relationship (001)κ || (001)γ
precipitates.distribution: uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix

size.value: 1.0 ± 0.4 nm (nano-sized, smaller than 1 nm in TEM)

microstructure_list.region: overall / bulk of the solution-treated rod

structures.number_of_phases: 2 (FCC austenite + BCC ferrite) plus κ-carbide precipitates
structures.overall_structure: After solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching the Fe30Mn11Al0.6C steel consists of FCC austenite plus BCC ferrite (about 30% by volume fraction); the austenite is fine-grained due to suppression of grain coarsening by the ferrite, with abundant twin boundaries, and contains nano-sized coherent κ-carbides uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix.

unmapped_findings: Measured chemical composition of the C-0.6 steel (Table 1): 0.63 C, 30.10 Mn, 11.11 Al, Bal. Fe (mass%), with density 6.65 g/cm³.

The 0.6%C steel has the highest work-hardening rate among the Fe30Mn11Al(x)C series, and unlike the other C contents it shows a monotonic decrease of work hardening rate with increasing true strain (along with the 30Mn steel).

In the 0.6%C sample nano-sized κ-carbides smaller than 1 nm are precipitated in the austenite phase; their fine size together with short-range ordering of C and Al leads to very weak κ diffraction spots in the SAED patterns.

Across all investigated compositions the maximum true stress σ_TS is nearly constant at about 1350 MPa and the fracture strength σ_FS at about 2150 MPa, essentially independent of alloying content and microstructure (the 0.6C values being 1330 MPa and 2115 MPa respectively).
